outline: Renal regulation of blood pressure and electrolytes
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 activity in mineralocorticoid-responsive renal cells impairs conversion of cortisol to cortisone. Cortisol can then activate the mineralocorticoid receptor, increasing sodium retention and potassium/hydrogen secretion despite suppressed renin and aldosterone.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy is evaluated for persistent hypertension and episodic muscle weakness. Laboratory studies show hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentration are both suppressed. A urinary steroid profile shows a markedly increased cortisol-to-cortisone ratio.
lead: Which molecular defect most directly explains this patient's findings?
correct: Reduced renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 activity, allowing cortisol to activate mineralocorticoid receptors
distractors: Gain-of-function epithelial sodium channels causing aldosterone-independent sodium reabsorption
CYP11B1 deficiency causing accumulation of deoxycorticosterone
Autonomous adrenal aldosterone secretion despite suppressed renin
Loss-of-function mineralocorticoid receptors causing renal sodium wasting
distractor_notes: Liddle syndrome causes gain-of-function ENaC activity with low renin and low aldosterone, but it does not impair cortisol-to-cortisone conversion or increase the urinary cortisol-to-cortisone ratio.

11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency can produce low-renin hypertension through deoxycorticosterone excess, but the defining biochemical defect is impaired adrenal steroid synthesis rather than failure to inactivate cortisol to cortisone.
Primary aldosteronism suppresses renin but has autonomous, inappropriately elevated aldosterone rather than the suppressed aldosterone in this stem.

Mineralocorticoid receptor loss causes pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 with impaired sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, producing salt wasting and hyperkalemia rather than hypertension with hypokalemia.
key_expl: The combination of early hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin and aldosterone, and an increased urinary cortisol-to-cortisone ratio indicates apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 normally converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone near the mineralocorticoid receptor. Loss of this enzyme permits cortisol to activate the receptor, producing sodium retention, volume expansion, potassium loss, and feedback suppression of renin and aldosterone.
objective: Recognize apparent mineralocorticoid excess from low-renin, low-aldosterone hypokalemic hypertension and an increased cortisol-to-cortisone ratio, and link it to loss of renal 11-beta-HSD2 activity.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI MedGen / Genetic Testing Registry
sources.title: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess
sources.support: NCBI MedGen defines apparent mineralocorticoid excess as low-renin hypertension with low aldosterone, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis due to deficient HSD11B2 activity, which decreases conversion of active cortisol to inactive cortisone and permits cortisol to activate the mineralocorticoid receptor.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Gene
sources.title: HSD11B2 hydroxysteroid 11-beta dehydrogenase 2
sources.support: NCBI Gene identifies HSD11B2 as 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and associates it directly with apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

sources.title: Testing for Endocrine Hypertension
sources.locator: Table 7 — Testing for Rare Causes of Endocrine Hypertension
sources.support: Endotext lists apparent mineralocorticoid excess with low renin, low potassium, low aldosterone, and increased urinary free cortisol/cortisone and cortisol-metabolite ratios, distinguishing it from Liddle syndrome and other low-renin states.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Liddle Syndrome (Pseudohyperaldosteronism)
sources.support: NCBI describes Liddle syndrome as gain-of-function ENaC activity causing sodium retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and suppressed renin and aldosterone.

sources.title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
sources.support: Endotext states that 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency permits deoxycorticosterone accumulation, which can cause sodium retention and low-renin hypertension with suppressed aldosterone.

sources.title: Overview of Endocrine Hypertension
sources.support: Endotext describes primary aldosteronism as autonomous aldosterone production that suppresses renin, distinguishing it from low-aldosterone pseudohyperaldosteronism.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus Genetics
sources.title: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that NR3C2 loss-of-function causes defective mineralocorticoid receptor signaling, reducing renal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion and producing sodium loss with hyperkalemia.
